From CIF to colliding slabs: anthracene and maleic anhydride

Every structure on this page was produced by the package's builder from the two CSD entries in the Diels–Alder project. The slab builder runs again in your browser from the same per-face motifs, so the sliders change real structures, not pictures.

ANTCEN anthracene C14H10 · MLEICA maleic anhydride C4H2O3 · UMA uma-s-1p2p1, task omc (CPU)
1 · read_cif

CIF sites become a crystal of whole molecules

The reader applies the operators listed in the CIF, merges copies that land on the same site, then follows bonds across the cell boundary so each molecule is in one piece with its centre of mass inside the cell.

drag to rotate · scroll to zoom

2 · bfdh · terminations · build_slab

Pick a face, a termination and a size

For each Miller plane the builder finds a reduced in-plane basis and a stacking vector one dhkl tall. Cut planes sit between molecular layers and are ranked by how many intermolecular contacts (< 4 Å) they break per nm². Molecules join a layer by their centre of mass, so no molecule is ever cut.

Where the cut goes: terminations as planes through the crystal

The oriented crystal seen edge-on (the (h k l) planes are horizontal; four repeats of dhkl are stacked). Molecules are coloured by molecular layer: molecules whose centres of mass sit at the same height along the normal. Every candidate cut plane is drawn: the selected termination solid, the others faint. A slab keeps the molecules whose centres of mass lie between its bottom cut and its top cut, the selected number of layers higher; everything outside is grey. The structures behind each property

Each property is a set of structures the calculator evaluates. These are those structures, generated the way the workflow generates them, followed by the UMA omc numbers from the runs on this machine.

Surface energies: cleaved and relaxed

Slabs at least 20 Å thick (3–5 layers) cut from the UMA-relaxed bulk; central layer fixed, both faces relaxed to 0.02 eV/Å. 21 slabs on the entropy cluster, about a minute each; maleic anhydride (1 0 0), (0 0 1) and (1 1 1) were added after the first run, and (1 0 0) T2 came out lowest of all its faces. Bold: the lowest termination of each face. Labels: relaxed γ (change on relaxing).

Crystal shapes: which faces win

face familyinputarea

How much does γ depend on the slab cell?

relaxed γcleaved γlinear fit of E_slab(n), relaxed
seriescellatomsγ mJ/m²

What changes γ, and what doesn't. Vacuum (10–30 Å): no change at all. UMA's 6 Å cutoff and lack of long-range electrostatics mean 10 Å already separates the periodic images. In-plane supercell (up to 2 × 2): under 1 mJ/m². Without a nudge a supercell relaxes exactly like the 1 × 1 cell, because nothing breaks its symmetry, so the supercells were also relaxed from atoms displaced at random by 0.1 Å; no reconstruction appeared. Thickness is the one that matters: thin slabs of anthracene (1 1 0) and maleic anhydride (1 0 1) read 2–4 mJ/m² high, and from 4–5 layers γ is within about 1 mJ/m². The linear fit of slab energy against layer count needs no bulk reference. For anthracene (1 1 0) it gives 96, not 92, because molecules inside the slab come out 3–4 meV lower than in the bulk cell. That points to a small cell-dependence in UMA's energy (not tested further). Taken together: treat γ as ± 2–4 mJ/m². Differences larger than that (anthracene (0 0 1) < (1 1 0); maleic anhydride (1 0 0), (1 0 1), (1 1 0) < (0 0 1), (1 1 1)) are robust; the order within maleic anhydride (1 0 0) ≈ (1 0 1) < (1 1 0) is not.
4 · which faces should meet

Exposed reacting groups, not just stable faces

For a Diels–Alder collision the faces that touch must expose anthracene's central ring (C9/C10) and maleic anhydride's C=C. On every relaxed slab the page highlights those atoms, and the table gives the tilt of the reacting ring (0° = lying flat) and how far the reacting group sits below the outermost atoms. Maleic anhydride (P2₁2₁2₁) is not centrosymmetric, so top and bottom faces can differ.

Candidate pairs on the UMA-relaxed cells

ANTCENMLEICAroleleast-strain cellDiels–Alder picksmallest cell
Recommended: anthracene (1 1 0) on maleic anhydride (1 1 0) T0. Anthracene (1 1 0) is its second most stable face and the largest by area, with the central rings closest to the surface (2.5 Å, against 4.4 Å on (0 0 1)). Maleic anhydride (1 1 0) T0 is within 5 mJ/m² of its most stable face and has the most exposed C=C of any low-energy face (about 1 Å down). Comparison run: anthracene (0 0 1), its real plate face, where the C9/C10 are buried and the impact has to disrupt the surface first.

Which coincident cell: the face pair can be joined through several cells, each with a fixed rotation of maleic anhydride. The least-strained one (0.81 %, 88.3°) crosses every C=C with the C9···C10 axes, so the Diels–Alder pick is the least-strained cell in which every contact site can line up: 1348 Å² at 0.99 %, maleic anhydride rotated −32.6°, built at its best registry. "aligned" counts contact sites with a C=C within 30° of parallel anywhere in the cell; "lined up" counts those with one also within 1.5 Å in plane at the best registry. Built in section 6.

A strong alternative: maleic anhydride (1 0 0) T2. It was not in the first set of faces, because the BFDH prediction ranks it 8th, but its relaxed γ (111.6 mJ/m²) is the lowest computed for maleic anhydride. On anthracene (1 1 0) its aligned cell (1452 Å², 1.17 %) lines up about twice the fraction of sites that (1 1 0) does (13 of 28 against 6 of 26). Its least-strain cell crosses every C=C, like (1 1 0)'s. For (1 0 0) and (0 0 1) the alternative terminations score the same, because the 2₁ axis along the surface normal makes their contact layers 180° copies of each other. The interface viewers below still use (1 1 0).
5 · molecule_removal_energy

Taking one molecule off the surface

Every distinct exposed molecule of a face (any atom within 3 Å of the outermost atom; copies under the surface lattice count once) is removed in turn from a relaxed, periodic slab with vacuum above and below, at least 15 Å across in plane so each vacancy is far from its periodic copies. Vertical: E(slab − m) + E(m, frozen) − E(slab), nothing relaxes. Vertical, relaxed surface: the same on the relaxed slab. Adiabatic: relaxed vacancy slab + relaxed gas molecule − relaxed slab, the desorption energy. Removing a molecule costs 2|Elatt| from the bulk and |Elatt| from a kink site, so a terrace molecule falls between the two dashed lines.

colours: exposed sites · pink: the molecule removed · grey box: slab cell

Removal energies per exposed site, kJ/mol

Hover a row to see that molecule in the 3D view; click to select it.

vertical (cleaved)vertical (relaxed surface)adiabatic

Vertical: the molecule is pulled out with nothing allowed to relax, the binding broken in a sudden event. Adiabatic: both ends relaxed (the vacancy slab, and the molecule to its gas-phase shape), the thermodynamic desorption cost; it is lower than the vertical value on the relaxed surface by the relaxation energy.

6 · match_lattices · build_interface · set_collision_velocities

Two crystals in one cell, ready to collide

Coincident supercells come from pymatgen's Zur–McGill search on the primitive surface cells; mirror-image matches are dropped and the strain is the polar decomposition of the in-plane map. Only molecular centres move with the strain, so no bond is stretched.

Rigid translation preview, not MD.
B's bottom face (h̄ k̄ l̄) meets A's top face (h k l). For the other orientation, build with flip_slab(b) before matching.

How the lattices are locked together: rotation, then strain

The rotation is not chosen for chemistry. It is the in-plane angle that brings maleic anhydride's matched supercell onto anthracene's (the R in F = R·U); after it, U stretches the cell by the lattice mismatch. Any other angle breaks the periodic match, so each coincident cell has one fixed angle; choosing the rotation means choosing the cell. The last column counts anthracene contact sites that have any maleic anhydride C=C within 30° of parallel to their C9···C10 axis, which no registry can change. Click a row to switch cells.

cell Å²mismatchrotation of Bsites with an aligned C=C

Registry: sliding maleic anhydride over anthracene to line up the reacting groups

Unlike the rotation, the sideways position (registry) of the top slab is free. Looking down on the contact: amber bars are anthracene C9···C10 axes in its top layer, teal bars are maleic anhydride C=C bonds in its bottom layer. A site counts as lined up when some C=C midpoint sits within the distance threshold of its C9/C10 midpoint in plane and the two axes are within 30° of parallel, the geometry of the Diels–Alder approach. The cell (and so the rotation) is the one chosen above, with the strain shared. This is a geometric guide, not an energy: it does not include the vertical separation or relaxation.


        

      

    

  


  
  

    
7 · interface_options · build_interface(repeat=…)
Choose the interface size

      
The atom count is the in-plane cell times each slab's thickness. Smaller coincident cells need more strain; any cell can be repeated at the same strain; each slab's thickness is set in whole layers. This explorer covers anthracene (1 1 0) on maleic anhydride (1 1 0) T0 on the UMA-relaxed cells, and builds every option in your browser from the same structures the Python code makes.

8 · the same thing in code
Reproduce this page

    


from MartiniFuncs.crystals import *

ant = read_cif("ANTCEN.cif")                       # P2₁/a, Z = 2, Z′ = 0.5
mal = read_cif("MLEICA.cif")                       # P2₁2₁2₁, Z = 4
bfdh(ant, max_index=2)[:5]                         # faces worth computing
terminations(ant, (0, 0, 1))                       # cut planes, fewest broken contacts first

a = build_slab(ant, (0, 0, 1), min_thickness=18)   # primitive in-plane cell for matching
b = build_slab(mal, (1, 1, 0), min_thickness=18)
m = match_lattices(a, b, max_area=1200, max_length_tol=0.04, max_angle_tol=0.04, sort="strain")[0]
interface = build_interface(a, b, m, gap=3.0, vacuum=16, strain_fraction=0.5)
set_collision_velocities(interface, 500.0, temperature_K=300)   # m/s, relative

# section 5: energy to take one molecule off the (1 1 0) surface
slab = build_slab(ant_relaxed, (1, 1, 0), min_thickness=20, min_lengths=15)
r = molecule_removal_energy(slab, calc, {"C14H10": e_gas}, lattice_energy=e_latt)

calc = crystal_calculator("uma", model="uma_data/uma-s-1p2p1.pt", task="omc")
# python -m MartiniFuncs.crystals.workflow ANTCEN.cif --calculator uma --task omc --out antcen_uma

    

  


  
Structures and numbers generated with MartiniFuncs.crystals (branch organic_crystals) and fairchem UMA uma-s-1p2p1 (task omc) on CPU. Bulk and gas relaxations ran on CPU; the 21 relaxed surface slabs (jobs 166553, 166960) and the slab-size study (jobs 166961, 166964) ran on the entropy cluster. The equation of state and elastic constants are set up but were not run for this page. Gas-phase references were recomputed without charge/spin settings, which UMA's omc head would otherwise read; this corrected the lattice energies (anthracene −99.4 → −106.7, maleic anhydride −103.3 → −76.3 kJ/mol).
